entry.title: Ego Free Journal
entry.content:
I made a mini-project where words you type disappear after a short period of time. I had the idea after reading something (I can’t remember where) which said that having everything recorded was giving us an outsized self of self and this was actually making us less happy. The reasoning being we can control a lot, but not everything, so that when things out of control don’t go our way we feel an oversized psychological wound.

So this is just a zen art project that imagines what a journal would be like if we had no sense of self, like if Shakespeare had written Hamlet just for himself then watched is dissolve away.

entry.title: Yet another AI retrospective
entry.content:
2026 was the year AI became the default way to write code across a lot of the industry - or at least in the web-dev, fast results commercial space I’ve spent my career working in. For me I’ve really tried to lean into using AI as well as possible (in no small part thanks to a one-off $1000 credit from Anthropic at work).

I’d like to share some my overall thoughts, some positive and some negatives then my thoughts on the future at the end.

To start with - I think AI is a net large positive both for the commercial software industry and for at home fun or artistic use. I still think as a whole, especially at work, we are fumbling around for the best possible usages for it. I’ve now had enough experience to see versions of this play out: big-data, no-sql and microservices come to mind as technologies that were rapidly adopted into innapriorpiate situations then loudly and vengefully dropped. AI feels more like The Cloud - initially mocked by some but it became more-or-less a better way for most organisations to operate.

My personal preference for using gen-AI to give some context

  • Opus tier models in virtually all cases
  • I still am the primary ‘typist’ for most non-trivial code I touch
  • Using AI to gather context and produce one-off reports is for me the biggest game-changer of the technology

I think the only thing controversial in this is not using AI to generate code in virtually all cases. While I have no actual numbers for this the results even with frontier models is still disappointing and doesn’t justify the often significant costs. Reading and writing are different fundamentally different skills. As anyone who has learned a language will tell you - you can feel like an expert in reading a language, but the even after the simplest conversations you’re reduced to a jabbering wreck. I think writing code isn’t so different. Having to really understand the domain and problem you are dealing with is for me the point of being a software engineer, by having to generate my own changes I can get a feeling for the current codebase, the product domain, that simply reading generated output doesn’t give me. I would still feel the superficial feeling of understanding claude can give you with its writing style is dangerous. But what I am not saying is that fumbling around trying to remember particular elegant language syntax or crafting some perfect code is still the most valuable use of my time - with a clear goal and limited context most AI models are now a better coder than I am.

So in summary - I find writing code to be the most efficient way of understanding what it is that I am doing. Others experiences may differ of course, I’m speaking for myself only.

Aside: “spec driven development”. I’ve basically always done this even before AI, but the old adage - No plan of action survives first contact with the main enemy body - still applies. You need to get down and dirty with the detail at some point, being immersed in it helps give the necessary context.

Opus/Sol all the way

Opus tier models are phenomenal coders but my experience is all models still are disappointing for routine non-trivial software development work. I’ve tried to replicate some of the results I’ve seen people on the internet claim at my job but most times have failed, often burning $50+ with nothing to show for it. This is really quite puzzling when you consider these companies are solving Millennium Maths problems with similar models, and yet at the same time they can still make a mess of a simple task.

My best results have come at the low end of the cost scale - small context windows, focussed tasks, rapidly restarting if context-rot seems to be setting in. In this scenario why use sonnet? Yes you might save a dollar or so, but at the cost of (generally) worse quality work.

Others have talked about this a lot but I still really hate how opus uses English. Its so long winded, verbose and hard to follow. My personal system prompt has an entire paragraph with a style guide just to make it bearable.

Is it possible to have too much productivity?

Even before AI came onto the scene it was widely acknowledged that software development is a mentally demanding job, and expecting 35-40hrs+/week of solid work is expecting too much, especially for over 25s. AI has (good) reduced to the need to do a lot of coding drudgery - e.g. setting up unit test cases, getting fiddly language specific features, refactoring. I have found though that this has meant you can spend the entire (non-meeting) day in the weeds of interesting but still challenging problems. Obviously no-one likes being bored at work but I’ve noticed increasingly that I have to sometimes give myself longer breaks - before a boring refactor might take 30 minutes but leave you recharged - now that job is already done.

I’m not sure where this leads. Probably nowhere but it’d be interesting to see if the industry, especially startups, become even more youth focussed.

Speed or haste and does code quality still matter now?

Most commercial software companies create an environment where speed is rewarded and highly praised. This is no bad thing in and of itself, companies want to make money and often new features are what makes money. But as a software engineer maintenance takes at least equal priority. So my experience is rooted in a time where reading code was really slow, and ‘spaghetti’ code was considered extremely harmful a large part because of how much code would have to be read by to understand it. AI really does change the picture here - by being able to trace a dizzying number of call sites and summarising them into a coherent story it can make a formerly un-manageable codebase approachable.

This is still I think the most amazing thing for me - being able to dispatch an agent to trace the behaviour of a API in another service, or summarise the behaviour of some impenetrable labyrinth of … unconventional … code is such a positive change compared to how it used to be.

So I’m wrestling with the question when doing PR reviews of AI code, namely: I don’t like this code, it is hard to understand and there’s about 10x too much to review ‘safely’.

But – seriously – does this still matter? If a developer is creating software by typing a compression of the code they want in an English sentence, and the AI is perfectly capable of compressing the existing codebase down into a form that’s changeable, does it matter that I cannot understand the change?

For me personally am I still of the opinion that yes, coding standards shouldn’t change and using AI to write more code is irresponsible at worst, and when compared to using it to the same amount of better code just plain inefficient. But am I right? I actually am doubting myself.

I think on the ‘slow down’ side the evidence is

  • Senior engineers (including myself) authoring code including novice mistakes
  • Noticeably more buggy interactions between systems as more change is put into the two sides or a contract (e.g. mobile vs browser, service-service)
  • I’ve noticed less flexibility in adjusting to changing requirements - e.g. because a single engineer can produce an app in no time, an early stage change in product requirements (natural) causes an outsided impact. Generally the code as always is the easiest thing to change, but I’ve seen much more of my time needing to go into complex database schema refactorings and data migrations than ever before.

I think the last point is the most fundamental. A code migration has always been ‘easy’ but the data migration is the challenge. Reducing the application tier coding time probably means even more emphasis on getting the schema right ahead of time.

I’ve noticed as well with “spec driven development” that we’re possibly moving back towards waterfall style work - when you can get production users in half the time, you’re also giving yourself half the time to spot issues with the data model - so you need to be even more sure what you’re doing is right before you start.

Slop grenades

The “slop grenade” (a colossal amount of low quality AI work) is an organisational problem. If you or your colleagues are routinely spamming low quality work and documentation to production, or worse ‘helping’ your colleagues with PR descriptions that ape a Dickensian sentence structure; toting vertiginous detail, compelling a thesaurus to fathom, then please stop forthwith. If you’re a senior you need to have these conversations, yes they’re uncomfortable but its your responsibility to use your expertise to guide the team.

And using AI to reply to your colleagues should not be OK. Forcing a human to argue with a next-token predicator is borderline abusive behaviour.

Wider trends and “big brain time”

Productivity and money

I said last year that I’d estimate AI giving engineers a 1-5% productivity increase. I think this is laughably too low, but really for senior engineers I think the productivity gain isn’t as high as is claimed. If someone says AI makes them 10x more productive I think that basically means they don’t understand productivity statistics. For context in a country like France, the productivity increase for farmers between 1900 (hand tools, horse drawn ploughs) to 1960 (modern fertlisers, tractors) would be something like 8-10x - and globally replicated this transformed human society in the most profound way it has ever changed. Claude code is cool but we’re not there yet, sorry.

The current economic picture seems to be becoming clear - a clear pickup in software companies productivity - good revenue, lower headcount, but at the cost of reduced hiring at the junior level. I’d say this matches my experience exactly - boring time consuming routine coding is now basically fully automated which means I genuinely get an appreciably larger workload done.

But the thing which interests me is how this is costed for. AI use on a large mature codebase can be really, really expensive i.e. >$1000/month. While its quite easy to get a lot of productivity for a lot less than this I am curious at the executive level how this is being seen. For example a senior engineer in London costs a company at least £10,000 (like $13500 probably) a month to hire. If said engineer spends $12,000/year on AI they have increased their cost to the company by ~10%. So you need a ~10% productivity increase to justify this. Remember that AI power users will go much above this. This is a little catty but my impression of tokenmaxxers believe they are 10x more productive - but actually are they? Certainly code is written many many times faster but does this always translate into productivity? My experience using a lot of tokens is that context rot is still a very, very real problem, and that using brain + AI makes it quite hard even to spend this much money. The other thought I had is because AI is still largely a USA product a company in a lower income country like Turkiye pays just as much as a London based engineer - meaning high AI use there is even more of a concern for the bill payers.

Lastly - I still think valuations for AI adjacent companies are bananas, but equally there’s another part of me that thinks maybe some time in the near future the AI models will become fully able to replace human labour, even for expensive office jobs. I think the other factor often overlooked is seeing a person compared to an AI. Lets say it costs an employer £120,000pa to employ a senior - the 120k buys you in the best possible case about 45-46 weeks of work. Unless they get sick, or have a child, or get depressed, or just lose motivation. Then if you don’t need them anymore you have to undergo an expensive and time consuming redundancy program, better hope you got everything right, otherwise you’re getting sued.

An AI agent seen in the same light is much, much more attractive in comparison. Full productivity always, no sick days, down to the millisecond at-will ‘employment’. It is like having an endless supply of gig workers at your beck and call. Uber for the professional classes. I think we need to be vigilante that we don’t let this technology erode hard won employment rights.

Politics

A common theme I’ve noticed when discussing AI (and technology in general) is that technologists often underestimate the importance of the political system or beliefs of the creators that creates a piece of technology on both itself, and its rollout. While its often the case that technology is influenced more by the natural laws of physics than human ones I feel software is a lot more politised than we might think. Certainly when talking to non-technologists who are critical of AI the recurrent themes are to talk mainly about the people creating the machines and their beliefs than what the AI is doing.

I think an interesting example of what I mean is dating apps, which have been created overwhelmingly by men, probably mainly because men are more likely to be coders. But its worth thinking about what the these apps show you - massive emphasis on photos, some optional questions to indicate personality. Who is more likely to rate partners mainly based only on looks? Men of course. I hope this isn’t cancellable but women tend to take in a broader range of factors when deciding on who they date than men - e.g. personality, humour, career, life plans… What could dating apps have looked like if they were built entirely by a group of women? It seems many complaints about dating apps stem for over-emphasis on looks - men feeling worthless, women feeling objectified.

While I think the potential for bias in AI prompts has been well covered by progressives its worth taking stock of the air we breathe - the way ChatGPT/Claude etc. talks reflects a highly western, individualist society. While I am inside this culture I can’t really critique it but for those outside I wonder if it is jarring? Secondarily the focus of AI to automate office work by the USA - for shareholder capitalist ends - seems to be contrasting with the Chinese focus on future tech like robotics. Its not a surprise Chinese people are more positive about AI than Americans who (clearly rightly) see the technology as a long-term threat to their prosperity and sense of pride at work.

Predictions

Strap in, I have literally no idea where this all goes.

entry.title: Totality
entry.content:
For he who knows how we are formed, he remembers that we are dust.

Psalm 103:14

I watched a total eclipse of the sun in the city of Vitoria in Northern Spain on the 12th August 2026 in what would be the most powerful, moving and profound experiences I’ve had for quite some time. I’ve struggled to put into words the feelings that caused me to actually cry for a minute or so afterwards but will do what I can here.

The sun was transformed into a black disc ringed by leaping flames for a few seconds in a display of ethereal - almost supernatural - beauty, what was once so familiar, so powerful, turned on its head. The last light of the sun was squeezed out bit by bit until nothing remained. The crowd of people gasped, cheered and hugged one another. Venus appeared low in the sky which had become blue like twilight. We all took off our glasses, looking directly at the sun with naked eyes. Then all too soon it ended, the crack of light returning and consuming the black disc and the sun roared back.

The physicality of our existence

A total eclipse exists because of cold coincidence due to the laws of gravity. A star forms from a gas cloud, ice and rocky debris gradually form into planets, those planets usually attract enough matter to form their own moons. Planets spin around the sun, moons spin around the planets. Our moon throws total eclipses our way in the way it does because it is just the right ratio of size and distance from the sun to just block it out for small sections of the planet every so often. If the moon were slightly larger they’d be common and almost routine, any smaller and we’d barely notice them.

A physical universe devoid of consciousness and humanity is a cold desolate place. How many eclipses have passed by when earth was a barren rock, how many with only single celled lifeforms to witness it. No, the light of a runaway nuclear explosion being briefly blocked could cause the somehow sentient products of ice and dust to feel joy and togetherness is something to be held on to.

Totality only lasts a few seconds from a fixed position on earth. The beauty, form and order of the event collapses and we return to normality. Like our own selves, a brief assembly of form, mind and love that comes together for too short a time before collapsing back into entropic disorder, all that physically makes us up scattering around the universe. But the beauty is not diminished by its brevity.

By the sweat of your brow you will eat your food until you return to the ground, Since from it you were taken. For dust you are and to dust you shall return.

Genesis 3:19

I truly do not see this as fatalistic or depressing. Whether you believe in God or not we do come from the dust, and we will return to it. The dust is us, the earth is us and even the universe is still us. There’s no separation.

The dust

The year of 2026 has been the worst I can remember for heat and drought in the UK. As a software engineer living an easy and cozy life it is all too easy to forget what I’ve just written. Seeing wildfires in the south of England has been shocking, as has the larger ones in the rest of Europe and across the world. While globally the year hasn’t been record breaking what feels different now is that this does not in any way feel like a one-off. That we will return in the rest of the decade to cool mid 20s, and a ‘heatwave’ is a day or two above 28C. It feels like this is just the beginning of something that will worsen and worsen as the years and decades progress. I’m not doomerist - I think as collective humanity can rise to the challenge, but a severe challenge it will be.

For he who knows how we are formed, he remembers that we are dust.

Seeing the a nuclear inferno in the sky disappear behind a ball of loose rock broke down some barriers I had around myself for a moment about my own, and all of humanity’s separation from the universe, about the need to grasp the time we have and protect the earth that we have emerged from.

I hope I can remember this, and yes I am aware of the irony of burning tonnes of aviation fuel to come to an eco mindset - but we should be able to find a balance of living a little and protecting nature (which is the same as protecting ourselves)

entry.title: AI is really killing the vibe

link.title: AI is really killing the vibe

entry.content:
Basically I like being a software engineer, and basically I like my weekly trips to the office to see my colleagues. Lately, however the vibes are just off. Not all the time, but often enough, we talk about AI.

Things should be good. I’m able to be more productive than ever. As an software engineer with 8 years experience I feel roughly in a good spot to have enough experience to not rush in and get burnt, but still being young enough to rethink my approach to software engineering in light of these new tools. But I feel about as pessimistic about the prospects for the industry as it’s possible to be, and basically everyone I work with feels the same. It’s not just feelings, my company has a hiring freeze yet still expects more output than ever, and layoffs across the industry are sending a chill down everyone’s spines. I think many of us are quietly guessing the years we have left.

For me the biggest feeling of horror and awe was experiencing a frontier model trivially do something that had taken my years to learn. From GPT-2 onwards AI writing code is not surprising, but seeing part of my identity and status be stripped away as some off the shelf model casually finds and fixes a complex concurrency bug in distributed systems, or uses deep knowledge of a programming language to solve some thorny issue was jaw dropping.

Our skills and knowledge have always given us meaning. I don’t know if it’s universal but English last names are very often trades - Smith, Tailor, Mason. An employable skill was so fundamental to our ancestors that they internalised it to the extent of making it their name. Having that seemingly stripped away from you is a shock. Having some machine casually do it and it not even be that hard can feel crushing.

First They Came For The Artists

I absolutely passionately hate AI art. I think it is a disgusting perversion of the human spirit. I’ll never forget the feeling of actual anger I felt the first time I saw a children’s book filled with AI slop. Don’t dare to dream kiddo, compressed inoffensive human expression is all you need!

But do I use AI art? Yes, definitely. Sometimes I just want a silly image to send to my friends to illustrate a point, sometimes it’s just fun seeing what will pop out and if it matches your imagination.

By way of an analogy I guess this is how managers are feeling about SWEs now. I’m sure most are actually quite nice people and recognise the work SWEs provide, but are under pressure to produce maximum value at minimum cost. Like the Charlatan who made a soulless children’s book for free, if you’re making a product quality and soul is tangental to the actual goal - profit. Worse - if you don’t wield the knife you might find yourself on the menu. So even if they don’t like it, and don’t want to do it, the disembodied decision making of a corporation will decide for them to “create operational efficiencies” when the time comes.

Rembrandt to make my point

Isn’t this all a bit crazy?

I know because I use it everyday AI is not taking my job just yet, and while it might have stopped some companies taking on graduate and junior developers I can’t seriously imagine anyone laying off a developer literally because of AI as things stand.

However the progress of this technology is showing no signs of slowing (remember when people thought GPT 4.1 was an amazing coding model?) and its hard not to feel anxious. What I’m telling myself for now is that unlike say hand weavers or switchboard operators we still have some value to add. The product of a SWE isn’t and hasn’t ever been purely code - it’s also communicating complexity clearly, building trust and understanding a complex domain. I personally can’t see non-technical people vibe coding production systems without some kind of human expert in the loop for the foreseeable future. I find the alternative vision of Sam Altman’s atomised, lonely one-person companies is corrosive to the soul - its people and interactions that will always be with us.

entry.title: The unexpected joy of looking at trees

link.title: The unexpected joy of looking at trees

entry.content:
I recently released I have become (or have always been) a total ignoramus when it comes to the natural world. Living in our urban world and increasingly digital world its easier to lose touch completely with anything natural in the environment.

So I set out to try and simply pay attention to and notice whatever nature is present in my corner of South East London. London is actually quite rich in plant life, given it is a large city, so is its a great place to start. From just looking you start to notice more and more variety and diversity, even on a boring city street.

With Machine Learning apps for identification like PlantNet it’s easier than ever to instantly identify whatever you are looking at with just a basic phone and no other knowledge.

But why is it a joy?

For me it’s mostly the feeling of connection to where you live. The trees you pass by are no longer random background assets; they have names like Limes, Horse Chestnuts, London Planes, Pin Oaks and Lebanese Cedars. Knowing something in some way brings it closer to you, makes it feel more familiar and personal to yourself.

You see why a tree might have been planted in the spot it was.

London Plane trees (a hybrid or the Oriental Plane and a Sycamore) is usually planted to line colonnades and walkways, providing high shade and cooling.

Pin Oaks - an American import - to create striking statement trees with a very ‘correct’ tree shape.

Cherry Trees - for their decorative blossom in spring

Maples - for their spectacular autumn displays of orange and red as the leaves fall.

You see things you didn’t expect

If you asked me if my local park had Pines and Cedar trees a little while ago I would never had said it did - and yet there they are, hidden in plain sight!

Around the entrance way to a beautiful memorial flower garden are planted a copse of Yew trees - a poignant and sombre reminder of death given their long association with graveyards in England.

Seeing the diversity of form of trees

It is a common misconception that trees are a group with a shared common ancestor - like mammals or lizards - but really they are a ‘form’ that many different very unrelated plant species have evolved to fill - an example of convergent evolution.

If you really look at leaves, even the local ones wherever you live, you’ll see an incredible difference in the approach to the same problem - maximise absorption of light when other species are trying to grab the light instead of you. Some leaves are compact, some leave large gaps, some are nothing but thin needle like limbs closely packed.

Seeing all this makes the world seem so much bigger than it did before, that there’s this buried complexity and beauty wherever you look for it.

entry.title: My Predictions for 2026
entry.content:
Predicting the future always goes well, which is why I’m going to give it a shot. Putting it on the internet for myself to shake my head at a year later will be even more gratifying.

But in all seriousness predicting things, even if the predictions are completely wrong, is useful in that it can allow you to reprioritise what you see as important, and what turns out to be from empirical evidence not so important while also showing what signals you completely missed.

AI & Technology

AI continues to impress technologically, but not in terms of dramatic productivity improvements in the software industry.

(N.b. by AI here I mean LLMs)
My reason for believing this is primarily personal experience. I am a software engineer working in a fairly typical Java development role, although skewed more towards writing new code vs maintenance and support.

I could not tell you which mid-senior developers that I work with are using AI tools and which are not (or using them minimally).

I personally find quite a lot of value in these tools so I found this a little surprising when I found this out. I had assumed everyone did as well, but several of my colleagues barely use AI and produce great work with no noticeable speed or quality difference. I’d put this down to a few factors

  • Intentionality: hand cranked code has been thoughtfully constructed from start to finish
  • Understanding: human written code is understood inside and out by the author, who can thoughtfully answer questions at code review, and consider full edge cases
  • Experience with IDEs can improve code generation speed vastly, and more experienced engineers will likely have learnt their tools well.
  • Context Rot: widely discussed but my personal biggest issue with LLMs when writing code - once going down the wrong track the tool stays there.
  • Over confident bug analysis and fix recommendation (i.e. wrong for complex problems)

Personally I’d estimate the benefit to a regular senior developer’s productivity from AI is around 1-5%. Seniors just do not spend enough time writing new code that the benefits there really move the needle; an AI cannot make a meeting go faster, speed up the process of deeply understanding code or carefully reviewing design documents.

For juniors the picture is different - it is immediately obvious who is using AI to generate code, but the downside is the generated code is often straight up wrong, misaligned to the actual problem or excessively verbose. However a junior using AI well is significantly more productive than someone who isn’t. Who is improving faster as an engineer is still up for debate though.

The AI ‘bubble’ does not pop.

AI improvements are not going to stop soon. While pristine training data is mostly all used up, “AI companies” have so much money now they can skirt this problem (see OpenAI hiring writers etc.). Optimisations to generation and model performance will keep the momentum high and investor interest going. That being said, I do not think this year will be as explosive as 2025.

Furthermore the tantalising prospect of AGI being just around the corner is unquantifiable but will be impossible to ignore.

The biggest risk this year is volatility, so much is invested in moonshots where any change to belief in the ability of relatively few numbers of people to deliver them will cause trillion dollar swings. As a thought experiment imagine an unlikely but possible event like Jensen Huang getting seriously ill - how much money would be lost?

The biggest risk longer term to OpenAI/Nvidia (and the whole financial system) are open weight models: Qwen, Deepseek, even Gemma. If the proprietary Silicon Valley models stop improving or open weight models reach a point where they are good enough, low cost providers can move in and host open weight models, potentially tailored to specific use cases. This would still likely help Cloud Computing companies like AWS, Google as they could run the inference of said models.

World Politics

A ceasefire in Ukraine

I have very little confidence in this but I believe peace could be reached. Trump and co have very many faults but their lack of moral standards could be an advantage in terms of getting peace. Realistically Ukraine regaining its lost territory right now is not happening so any peace deal has to reflect the military reality (unfortunately).

If Russia’s complicated masterplan fails which I think it will - continue playing Trump, help get Russia friendly far right governments elected across Europe, and defeat the still formidable Ukrainian armed forces significantly - I could see a curveball coming in the form of the Russian people saying “we’ve won, let’s have peace” and a painful deal letting them occupy some Ukrainian territory could be reached.

Until then I don’t think Putin will back off from trying to win outright.

Unending misery for Gaza and Palestine

I see absolutely no cause for optimism here. While hopefully direct hostilities are averted, the idea of the current extremist Israeli government managing the reconstruction of Gaza with perfect respect of Palestinian rights is hard to believe. The situation in the “Occupied Palestinian Territories” will continue on its seeming path to eventual annexation. It seems like the dream of a two state solution is dying.

The UK

The UK economy barely grows

I think the central issue is not the government, it’s the people. The public (who are significant for elections) do want growth but only if

  1. It does not inconvenience anyone, in any way whatsoever.
  2. It does not change anything in any way whatsoever.
  3. If change is impossible to stop, it must benefit those affected materially no matter how little the impact.

Being empathic this is understandable. Why should anyone have to put up with the annoyance of construction or the change to their environment if it doesn’t benefit them?

For me the wider issue is: we have through good intentions broken the feedback loops that hold the economy together.

  • If house prices increase this does not spur new building in fact local opposition increases to new developments as these are blamed for the gentrification
  • If more people move to an area the local government seems unable to raise the funds to improve infrastructure that would reduce the impact on locals (e.g. better roads, public transport etc.)

This is why we have absurd situations where local objections such as “my view will be spoiled when I walk my dog” are seriously raised. Being slightly more Chinese (or at least French) in our approach to infrastructure and housing will be needed to materially improve growth rates. How to get there is the hard part because it involves stripping away rights.

Another issue is the relentless online negativity pushing away potential skilled immigrants, investment and driving down consumer confidence which could actually materially reduce growth.

Labour does terribly in elections and resurrects Brexit as an issue

OK everyone knows Starmer’s Labour are going to struggle this year and have to pull a rabbit out of a hat to survive.

What I can guess at is that reversing some of Brexit will feature more and more prominently. Either Starmer will pick this up to try and save his government (unlikely as it will go against the immigration reduction stuff he’s been doing), or someone else will. This will cause a massive rupture because it will resurrect the central issue of Brexit, those who want Brexit but “done right” and those who don’t want it at all.

England Win the World Cup

Great squad, great manager let’s go. Surely this is one of the best chances for some time?
entry.summary: Predicting the future always goes well, which is why I’m going to give it a shot. Putting it on the internet for myself to shake my head at a year later will be even more gratifying.

entry.title: Jordan
entry.content:
Late November 2025: Jordan

For a long time in my life I’ve really wanted to visit the Middle East, mainly stemming from memories of long hours as a kid clicking away on Rome Total War, fighting the Selucid Empire, or sweeping in as the Parthian cavalry. As a Phoenician-stan the country I’ve wanted to visit the most has been Lebanon, but due to the security situation around Israel I thought it best to go further afield.

Jordan was overall a great choice, it’s extremely safe, has a long and rich history and some of the most unexpectedly delicious food I’ve almost ever encountered. It’s actually pretty easy to solo travel should you wish as well, with comfortable tourist buses taking you around the country. I thought Jordan was a richer country so the main downside is the begging (sometimes low key scamming), and poor treatment of animals.

Amman

I was actually quite impressed by Amman. I probably wouldn’t say its worth going there for its own sake, there’s some cool things to do, good food and interesting history.

It was also my first experience in a middle eastern city, so a new(ish) experience hearing the call to pray being absolutely blasted out at hair metal volumes. Overall it felt a safe city to walk around in and explore, although at times difficult without a car (e.g. dashing across 4 lane highways to get to a cornershop)

My taxi lift into Amman from the airport was also interesting. The driver initially didn’t talk but then ended up explaining a lot of their life - working in construction in Saudi but then returned to Jordan because of the labour conditions, initially working in tourism but having to drive uber because of the slowdown as a result of the Israeli wars. Some choices phrases as we discussed how Jordan was totally safe and tourists were wrong to stay away

  • The missiles flying overhead didn’t land anywhere near the cities!
  • The Syrian war is largely finished! Iraqis are too stupid to do anything other than kill each other!

But he was a nice guy and meant well. Jordan is a little bit of a police state but is safe at least.

Wadi Rum

Wadi Rum is where the main touristing gets going. Like a lot of Jordan it seems totally dependent on tourism, with the ‘Bedouin Camps’ being a varying degree of luxury fixed structures far away from the small town where the workers live with their families. It is strange seeing an obviously proud people having to work in tourism and you can feel the resentment bubbling under the surface at times, as well as being extremely patriarchal (I barely saw a woman).

That all being said the geography is absolutely stunning. It is perhaps burnished like Los Angeles by being such a commonly filmed location, with the vistas being instantly recognisable from films like Dune, Star Wars, The Martian and of course Lawrence of Arabia.

Jordanian tourism ‘weird tat shops’

As an aside, the most unexpected thing about the trip was the sheer number, and in-avoidability of the tourist tat shop, selling goods at maybe 5-10x the price anywhere else. For example it might cost £3 for a single water there, then in a petrol station just £0.25, but the main attraction was just random crap. It sounds mean but it was just random ‘stuff’ and all the buses would drop you off at these places and just sit around waiting 20 minutes hoping you’d buy something.

It was at its most extreme in Wadi Rum where even though the whole place is incredibly impressive, there’d be the mandatory stop-off at the ‘famous rock’ or ‘big dune’ that also coincidentally had a random tourist tat tent next door! I get developing countries need to monetise tourism, but this felt excessive and almost comical.

Petra

I’m not going to spend so long on Petra because of course it’s so well known and recognisable. Right now is actually a good time to go because it wasn’t so crowded and felt like slightly more of an intimate experience, although of course around the entrance it can still get crowded.

It is still incredibly impressive.

A slight downer is the use of animals to move people and cargo around. Mules are still likely the best choice to carry things up the steep paths, but in my opinion there should be restrictions on the wight of the people they carry. Obese individuals should be banned from using them, it is just cruel.

Madaba and Jerash

Last of all I visited too more cities on the tourist trail, Madaba which is the largest Christian population in Jordan, and Jerash which houses an enormous Roman ruin.

Madaba trades of the ‘city of mosaics’ tagline which it absolutely deserves. It is also a calmer, more relaxed city with some beautiful churches and even a tiny Roman Catholic population.

Unfortunately this beautiful mosaic depicting locations in the holy land was defaced by iconoclastic Muslims for depicting human faces long ago in the past.

Jerash is well worth a visit and easy to get to using the tourist buses, although it is best to book in advance. I found it difficult to take a photo of, but in person the sheer scale of the site (like Petra) is a little overwhelming.

entry.title: More things I’ve learned about developing enterprise software

link.title: More things I’ve learned about developing enterprise software

entry.content:
In the past year I’ve become increasingly senior at my job, being pushed into more engagement with various stakeholders at a large, UK fintech. While earlier in my career I worked very closely with product managers and leadership at a much smaller company, there’s a world of difference to working with large teams who are extremely removed from software development.

This post tries to encapsulate what I’ve learned, or has further been reinforced recently.

‘Soft’ Skills

Soft Skills as you become more senior (unless you’re a super specialised developer) become probably more important than tech ones, or at least the line becomes horribly blurred, for doing your job.

Understanding different ways of thinking

Engineers have a different mindset to business stakeholders

For business stakeholders the main reason for praise/prestige tends to be around identifying problems.

Engineers are praised for solving problems.

Trying to get a mix of both is crucial - but doing too much of one and not enough of the other is an issue. Too much problem identification tends towards circular conversations without a resolution. Engineers diving too soon into coming up with solutions can risk creating fixes to problems that don’t really exist - or even worse than that building subtly incorrectly mis-modelling real world business logic.

Here team work and effective communication is crucial. All meetings should have an intended outcome, and engineers should either understand the domain well enough to model it correctly, or product managers need to step in.

Dealing with timelines

Engineering is unusual in that success is based on timelines rather than outcomes. This is an endless problem that everyone struggles with, because generally we create a thing and it’s just assumed to be essentially bug free, highly available and easy to modify and change. It’s important to stress that (especially as a company’s tech stack grows and matures) that this stuff isn’t “free” and will require work. This can stray into coming up with Non-Functional Requirements - which in my opinion are showing things going slightly wrong, because it’s a kind of imposition of restrictive categoric data onto what is often quite ephemeral. I.e. do I feel this software is nice to work with?

The best way lies in building up personal relationships and trust between you and others and hoping that your judgement and expertise will be trusted. If it’s not, and it’s impossible then you potentially work at a chop shop and it’s time to move on. In the worst case pushing back more aggressively with comments meant to illustrate the difficulty of delivering to timelines can help (but be careful) e.g. It would be unfair to ask you (sales) what exactly what date you expect to sign (customer) because we are interested in outcomes rather than timelines. The idea here is to point out an absurdity we often see e.g. in March having a conversation where you commit to having features 1..50 on the spreadsheet all being in place at 9AM on the 17th September.

Stakeholders abhor a vacuum

So this is something I’ve seen over and over again in my career. The nature of software development work (especially at early stages of a project but really throughout) means it’s hard to communicate what’s really going on. Often it can look from the outside like no progress is being made - in early stage design, during periods of heavier refactoring - then suddenly everything happens at once.

The issue is that if you’re not upfront about what’s going on business leaders will often assume the worse, especially if you’re not in a high trust environment. What’s being asked for is so so often totally reasonable - just a few bullet points about what the team has been doing, what’s been challenging etc.. In many cases ‘micromanagement’ comes from this communication vacuum, where a middle manager isn’t certain of what’s happening, is being leant on my a senior manager who has no idea what’s happening. If you can send bite sized chunks of useful information up that chain it’ll keep managers happy and off your back. (In an ideal world)

Looking after developers in your team (if not a people manager)

It’s vital to learn how to delegate well. 9 times out of 10 people don’t know exactly what you’re doing, or even how best to help you with the workload - you can’t just drop work onto people’s lap and immediately expect them to get started. Delegation can often take time away initially but pays itself back over time.

Give Praise: This one is huge, especially for new starters or people who may lack confidence. Software Engineering can be lonely at times, and quite negative

  • Dealing with customer reported issues
  • Pushing back on timelines and “disappointing” other people in the business
  • An often challenging and esoteric job we do a lot of in isolation

In a way that may not be obvious people (especially but not exclusively juniors) have massive imposter syndrome which can become a deeply negative feedback loop.

  • I’m not good enough to do this work
  • So I’ll do something else, or not trust my judgement and get someone else to do the hard parts
  • So I don’t improve and gain confidence
  • So my imposter syndrome sticks around

While doing a kind of Big Tech AI Wow - What an interesting and intelligent insight that gets right to the heart of … doesn’t help anyone because its obviously disingenuous - remembering to give praise where its earned makes a huge difference. For example if you’re reviewing a PR that has a couple of minor issues but is overall OK then remember to include the praise for the 90% that’s good. Dropping a comment to praise specific things you think are smart can also give a lot of encouragement.

Technical Learnings

Do not ever drift along and push ‘First draft’ code into production

If I think about what’s gone well in the past year compared to what’s gone badly its when a “rough and ready” prototype has survived all the way into production, only to become a giant pain in the neck but increasingly hard to modify as customer data builds up.

The issue is basically down to not building a data model that makes sense and/or a set of abstractions that match the kind of behaviour you’re looking for your application. Why this happens tends to relate to:

  • timelines that don’t (seem to) give developers time to refactor and re-model code to make better,
  • a lack of teamwork where no-one feels empowered to make sweeping changes so an inferior design persists,
  • developers not understanding the product domain well enough.

All you can do yourself is fight this if it happens - push back if necessary (every time I’ve done this business stakeholders have been totally happy) to give pauses in feature delivery to make tactical and thoughtful changes for a couple of weeks. In your team be the change you want to see - try and build working relationships and a high trust environment (own up to mistakes, be friendly and share credit). For design work if no-one is stepping into that role - great that means you’re up and it’s the best way to learn. If your plans crash and burn at least you’ve learned something!

In my experience knowingly putting a design developers aren’t happy with in production is the worst way to tank team morale, delivery and trust with the rest of the business.

Time saved in testing is paid for many times over

This one is pretty simple and kind of a no-brainer. Test as many paths as is practical, especially, especially the unhappy paths. Add good automated ‘integration tests’ that test flows as a whole from the perspective of the end-client (e.g. a mobile device) to see if the disparate parts of your application are well glued together. Sending silly mistakes into non-prod environments that need to be reverted just wastes time.

Never send code to production you haven’t given a manual once over in demo.

The other risk for you personally as a senior developer is that you are “on-call” as far as many non-developers in the business are concerned. For example even if a bug or issue in production originates in a part of an application you have no idea about, you’re the one who’s going to be contacted about it because people know who you are. This can be a real mental burden and result in excessive context switching and exhaustion. This is why it is vital and in your own personal interest to keep as many issues off production as you possibly can.

Overseeing implementation of something you’ve designed, but are not the primary implementer for.

The example: This year I designed an async process that was a version of the classic manager/worker pattern where a series of tasks happen and eventually some entity is pushed through a state machine. To ensure consistency each worked could only make one transactional write to the database after fetching some data or making a modification to a remote service.

This is something I’ve found difficult. At earlier stages of my career what I’ve done tended to be smaller bit of functionality of APIs with a different defined purpose and scope, but as I’ve become more senior the complexity and impact of work increases. What I’ve found works well

  • Sharing very high level designs and flows using diagrams and docs. There’s not too much point going into detail at this stage as everything is so likely to change.
  • Making an initial implementation and personally creating the most crucial building blocks
  • Then ASAP have another developer extend your system, or implement interfaces required by it and get honest feedback. This is so crucial it’s hard to overstate. Software is often worthless until someone else touches it. No plan of software attack survives first contact with someone else to paraphrase Von Moltke.
  • Be vigilant but not overbearing at the review stage and ongoing monitoring.
    • At the review stage ensure the most fundamental parts of the design are being adhered to, but some freedom if it doesn’t affect the overall behaviour of the interface.
    • Often a developer (usually senior) will not understand the design and do something that violates its purpose. A senior on the team then wrote code that mixed fetches from other services, and multiple transactions, missing that the point was to avoid a situation where one system is up, the other is down and we update data into an inconsistent state. Being a senior the more junior reviewer waved the change through (perhaps thinking maybe they know something I don’t).
    • The issue here is that even if you document everything, explain it, there’s no guarantee that someone with too little time will come in and do something you don’t want. It’s your responsibility to check up and make sure you’ve done as much as you can to stop this happening.
  • Take criticism seriously but not personally. It’s extremely easy to criticise someone else’s code but this may or may not be useful criticism. It’s genuinely hard to take bad faith criticism from a colleague but try not to let it get to you. Some personal anecdotes
    • This system is too over-engineered and hard to use - seems like good feedback, but really the developer didn’t fully understand the process and was just trying to slam some code in. Writing better documentation and personally explaining things helped here.
    • This is too hard and time consuming to setup tests for. Ding ding: this is a huge problem and requires immediate attention to resolve. You should under no circumstances be making it hard for developers to test, because this will hammer the test coverage of new code. Resolution: Implement and refactor test preparation to make setup easy and simple, for example using a test specific data model of your system’s entities.

Read, read and then read some more

I cannot overstate this enough. I would say that reading software and business books (even if tangentially related) is maybe not super exciting, but is maybe the best use of your time outside work. Once writing code is ‘easy’ the best way to upskill yourself is by reading well regarded software books. You don’t have to agree with everything these books contain, but should at least find something interesting in their pages. Some books I’ve read recently and enjoyed

  • Designing Data-Intensive Applications: Martin Kleppmann (If you work with web applications you owe it to yourself to read this)
  • Why Machines Learn: Anil Ananthawamy (A segue to be sure but a clear and understandable dive into how machine learning actually works without getting lost in a sea of Python - quite Mathematical)
  • A Philosophy of Software Design: John Ousterhout
  • The Pragmatic Programmer (Legendary book on “Blue Collar” coding)
  • Everything is Predicable: Tom Chivers (OK not at all related but a really readable fairly lightweight book on Bayesian statistics that I’d recommend to anyone)

N.b. AI: I didn’t use AI to write this. So much intelligent stuff has been written about AI in software I don’t feel I have anything to add. I do feel though, for being creative, AI can hurt rather than help, as it (out of the box) tends to homogenise thought rather than let whatever you have that’s unique come out. For coding though it is obviously a productivity boon.

While earlier in my career I worked very closely with product managers and leadership at a much smaller company, there’s a world of difference to working with large teams who are extremely removed from software development.

entry.title: Surprising problems with S3 and Java’s InputStream

link.title: Surprising problems with S3 and Java’s InputStream

entry.content:
To begin with S3 is of course AWS’ object storage system that abstracts the underlying realities of actually storing files into a (mostly) intuitive and easy to use API. It’s reliability and reach are truly staggering and it is one of the most impressive large scale software systems out there.

But it can go wrong - there are some behaviours that are unclear, confusing and difficult. This is a list mainly composed of painful lessons learned the hard - code that seems innocuous but turns around to bite you when you least expect it. This is totally from the perspective of using the Java client SDK.

InputStream (more like PainPipe)

InputStreams are a fundamental abstraction for working with byte data with the JVM from the very outset of the platform and are deeply ingrained in all sorts of libraries. They are, it’s fair to say, ubiquitous.

With AWS S3 however the client gives you a nice Java bit of code like InputStream inputStream = s3Client.getObject(GetObjectRequest.builder().bucket("b").key("k").build())

Then a Java developer can see something like this and write some code like

try (InputStream inputStream = s3Client.getObject(GetObjectRequest.builder().bucket("b").key("k").build())) {
    byte[] buffer = new byte[1024];
    for (int length; (length = inputStream.read(buffer)) != -1; ) {
        byte[] bytes = new byte[length];
        var string = new String(bytes, StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
        // check something about the string
        if (string.contains("something-we-dont-like")) {
            throw new RuntimeException("Uh oh");
        }
    }
} catch (IOException ioException) {
    throw new RuntimeException(ioException);
}

I’ve seen code like this in production environments and in an ordinary situation in the JVM it is totally 100% OK. The try() syntax gives a guarantee that the stream will be closed.

Another example here might be if JSON objects are being stored in S3 and read into memory - if the application POJO ‘schema’ becomes incompatible with what’s stored in S3 then you’d see this a lot.

What is wrong with this?

The key is when the exception gets thrown. S3 is a remote server with a connection managed by HTTP! The JVM can close your stream sure, but what happens to the underlying connection? How does the multiple layers in technology know the connection is now severed? They don’t really. All that’s happened if some piped data is not being read anymore. Will it be read again soon? The actual HTTP connection has to wait for the default timeouts to expire before closing the connection.

It really can catch people out that close here does not mean closing the HTTP connection!

In a busy application then what can go badly wrong is a Java application might create a S3 client as a singleton with a fixed thread pool (say 50 or 100 threads). If these threads are all idling because of some nasty bug released in some code that parses S3 bytes then you can quickly get thread pool exhaustion, even if the code is ‘correct’ that throws the exception down the stack!

What could be done?

  1. Call the abort() method on ResponseInputStream
  2. Write all data to RAM or disk everytime
  3. Do not throw when processing S3 input streams.

There’s no perfect solution in my opinion.

For 1) the issue is you can get some messy code e.g. in that example I showed earlier say I add an abort like so

if (string.contains("something-we-dont-like")) {
    inputStream.abort();
    throw new AnImportantException("Uh oh");
}

In most cases this should be fine, but have to be aware that the abort is itself of course having to manage the underlying HTTP connection. There’s a lot of moving parts there and they can and will. This means the exception (or just anything) in the next line isn’t guaranteed to throw, which can introduce regressions in some code bases.

The other subtler issue is slight vendor lock in. In theory the beauty of using a system like S3 is allowing developers to insulate themselves from the harsh reality of actually putting things onto a disk, and this level of specificity to AWS’ system is perhaps replacing one form of “essential knowledge” (how a disk works) with another “AWS internals”. When you write Java code like this you would no longer be passing around the widely accepted InputStream into your applications you’d be passing an AWS interface with special error handling rules.

For 2) this is probably the best outcome. If you’re just piping to RAM or disk then there’s far less chance anything can go wrong when downloading the data, meaning shorter connections. There will be issues with risk around OOMing your application or running out of disk space (probably why InputSteam downloads were used in the first place) but the trade-off is worth it in my opinion. How much does adding disk space or even RAM add to running an application? Is it more or less than the salary-time it takes for someone in management to share their screen in an all hands?

For 3) it is so absurd to talk about, I only included to hit the “rule-of-3” in rhetoric.
entry.summary: To begin with S3 is of course AWS’ object storage system that abstracts the underlying realities of actually storing files into a (mostly) intuitive and easy to use API. It’s reliability and reach are truly staggering and it is one of the most impressive large scale software systems out there.

entry.title: My favourite 5 Books I’ve read in 2024

link.title: My favourite 5 Books I’ve read in 2024

entry.content:
To be clear these are not books published in 2024, just one’s that I have read this year.

5) Fermat’s Last Theorem - Simon Singh

This book is pretty much the gold standard for all popular science writing and definitely the most engaging book written on number theorists ever. I’m amazed it’s taken me so long to get around to reading it. It concerns the long journey to understand a childishly simple conjecture - is there a value n were a^n+ b^n = c^n - i.e. if you take some number n - say 511 are there three other different whole numbers where this equation holds?

Despite number theory - i.e. the mathematics of ‘whole numbers’ and how they relate (think Prime Numbers, whole number sequences etc.) being one of the least obviously applicable to the ‘real world’ the author does an absolutely sublime job in bringing the subject to life.

Where this book is above and beyond its peers is that it’s all too common for PopSci to become an extended summary of research or individuals and you lose sense of why the work is important and the context around it. There’s an excellent explanation of what Mathematical proofs really are - i.e. knowing that some numeric logic is true or false and the history and evolution of proofs throughout time. We even get a brilliant section of Godel and the limits of what its even possible for mathematics to do.

Other than that the prose is highly engaging, funny at times and deeply readable with enough depth that even people with good mathematical knowledge would find it fun to read, while bringing along those who maybe only took a GCSE.

4) The Dark Forest - Cixin Liu

This is Book 2 in the ‘Three Body Problem” series by Cixin Liu (or Liu Cixin, or just “Big Liu” idk) now being adapted by Netflix. For me it was my favourite. Book 1 is the most grounded in the real world, Book 3 disappears into utterly speculative fiction whereas this book stays as a description of plausible future societies and events. They’re all good but this book landed the hardest even though it is probably the most GrimDark version of the universe I’ve ever read. (Spoilers; The reason the universe looks dead is because any civilization that makes a ‘sound’ is immediately wiped out).

In summary the plot concerns humanity’s attempts to survive in the face of impending conquest by a more technologically advanced civilisation. There’s repeated references to 19th and 20th century China’s failure to adapt and survive to a world where it was no longer the most powerful country, which for a Western reader added an interesting cultural dimension to the novel. Interesting as well that Cixin Liu never makes moral statements, just takes a quite macho line that humanity needs to be stronger to survive. It is also so macho it becomes a little misogynist at times - good luck Netflix in the adaptation!

3) The Meat Paradox - Rob Percevil

An actually good and interesting book about the Meat/Veganism/Climate apocalypse debate. Without blame or name calling the author takes a look at humanity’s relationship with meat from hunter-gatherer societies to the present day. There aren’t really any easy answers, but squeamishness around eating meat appears to have followed us from our earliest evolutionary history. In a way this makes sense - we are social creatures and if we have empathy for one another it makes sense we have empathy with those “like us”.

It also refuses to sweep under the rug the health benefits many people have (me included) from eating meat (I’ve tried just eating only veg and I get ill the whole time), as well as the challenge of “Big Tech” solutions not providing nutrition.

2) Orbital - Samantha Harvey

An absolutely beautiful novel about life on earth when pushed into the harsh extremes of the International Space Station. The idea of a spaceship as an extended allegory for the earth is not new, it dates back to the 1970s with the first full colour images of earth taken by the Apollo Moon missions, but this is one of the most subtle and profound takes on the subject matter. It’s also refreshing to be reminded of just how amazing the ISS is in many ways - a population of humans living beyond our atmosphere, and how mundane most of what astronauts actually do is. The metaphor which is reinforced by descriptions of a giant Typhoon - is that we need to treat Earth like living in a spaceship (i.e. with great care) because we really are floating in space. The novel makes this much more profound than I’ve done!

That being said there’s no real plot as the novel just describes a few ‘days’ onboard the ISS and nothing dramatic or exciting happens but the writing and characterisation is so strong it holds it all together.

1) The Player Of Games - Iain M Banks

Space Operas may be immature but they are an absolute delight to read. No need to explain how ‘hyperdrives’ work, how these bizarre civilisations actually function, why there are always sexy cat ladies, just pure adventure.

This novel, book two in the “Culture” series has the best player of board and strategy games in the galaxy take on a special request to compete in a game series an empire of aliens use to select their leader. Essentially everyone (or at least lots of people) in a space empire plays a massively complex strategy against each other until finally one emerges as their emperor. It is totally silly when you explain it but the novel pulls it off.

I’ve said it before and I’ll say it again, playing games is a great way to understand someone’s personality - do they make bold moves and hope for the best? Turtle and try and stockpile? Make alliances? And in some ways this book is like a love letter to strategy wargaming (Yes I’m cool). The ‘lore’ in describing a future society (The Culture) watched over by superintelligent computers focussed on maximising human happiness and how it interacts with a ‘barbaric’ expansionist empire is fascinating. What’s acceptable to do to try and help such a society develop given a direct approach will antagonise the population? What role do humans play in events if Super-AI is orders of magnitude more intelligent? Would a Super-AI experience the real world more like a game with (with enough intelligence) seeing predictable patterns driving behaviour where we see chaos?

It also includes may favourite use of pathetic fallacy maybe ever where the most dramatic and climatic board game showdown literally happens at the same time as a continent sized firestorm is approaching towards the arena. Talk about upping the stakes!
entry.summary: To be clear these are not books published in 2024, just one’s that I have read this year.
